author: Simone Weil
source: The Iliad, or the Poem of Force
text: Force is that x that turns anybody who is subjected to it into a thing.

author: Simone Weil
text: The evil we do is obscured and embellished by imagination.

author: Iris Murdoch
text: I can only choose within the world I can see, in the moral sense of "see" which implies that clear vision is a result of moral imagination and moral effort.

author: Iris Murdoch
text: The self, the place where we live, is a place of illusion. Goodness is connected with the attempt to see the unself.

author: Iris Murdoch
source: Metaphysics as a Guide to Morals (1992)
text: Man is a creature who makes pictures of himself and then comes to resemble the picture.

author: Iris Murdoch
text: Anything which alters consciousness in the direction of unselfishness, objectivity and realism is to be connected with virtue.

author: Iris Murdoch
text: Moral change and moral achievement are slow; we are not loosely and lightly attached to the world.

author: Hannah Arendt
text: Power corresponds to the human ability not just to act but to act in concert.

author: Hannah Arendt
text: Promises are the uniquely human way of ordering the future, making it predictable and reliable to the extent that this is humanly possible.

author: Hannah Arendt
text: Storytelling reveals meaning without committing the error of defining it.

author: Elizabeth Anscombe
text: The concepts of obligation, and duty—moral obligation and moral duty, that is to say—and of what is morally right and wrong, and of the moral sense of "ought," ought to be jettisoned if this is psychologically possible.

author: Elizabeth Anscombe
text: It would be a great improvement if, instead of "morally wrong," one always named a genus such as "untruthful," "unchaste," "unjust."

author: Elizabeth Anscombe
text: What distinguishes actions which are intentional from those which are not? The answer that I shall suggest is that they are the actions to which a certain sense of the question "Why?" is given application.

author: Elizabeth Anscombe
text: Intentional action is action with a certain description under which it is intentional.

author: Elizabeth Anscombe
text: The greater part of modern moral philosophy derives from Sidgwick and is utilitarian or consequentialist.

author: Philippa Foot
text: Moral evil is a kind of natural defect.

author: Philippa Foot
text: Virtues are in general beneficial characteristics, and indeed ones that a human being needs to have, for his own sake and that of his fellows.

author: Philippa Foot
source: Moral Beliefs (1958), in Virtues and Vices
text: We are not free to say that just anything is the subject of a moral belief.

author: Philippa Foot
text: There is no criterion for determining what is good for a human being that is independent of the nature of the human being.

author: Philippa Foot
source: The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect (1967)
text: We are most of us inclined to think that a great deal of damage, and even lives lost, is better than doing murder.

author: Martha Nussbaum
text: Luck can intervene between a person and the living of the good human life.

author: Martha Nussbaum
text: The capabilities approach asks not only about people's total or average well-being but about what each person is able to do and to be.

author: Martha Nussbaum
text: Emotions are not just the fuel that powers the psychological mechanism of a reasoning creature; they are parts, highly complex and messy parts, of this creature's reasoning itself.

author: Martha Nussbaum
text: Narrative imagination is an essential preparation for moral interaction.

author: Damascius
source: Damascius, Life of Isidore (via the Suda), on Hypatia
text: She was devoted to philosophy and explained it publicly to anyone who wished to hear.

author: Synesius of Cyrene
source: Synesius of Cyrene, Letter to Herculianus (testimonium on Hypatia)
text: She honorably presides over the mysteries of philosophy.

author: Christine de Pizan
source: The Book of the City of Ladies (1405), I.1
text: There is not the slightest doubt that women belong to the people of God and the human race as much as men.

author: Christine de Pizan
source: The Book of the City of Ladies (1405)
text: Just as women's bodies are softer than men's, so their understanding is more sharp and clever.

author: Christine de Pizan
source: The Book of the City of Ladies (1405), I.27
text: Not all men (and especially the wisest) share the opinion that it is bad for women to be educated.

author: Edith Stein
text: Empathy is a kind of experiential act sui generis.

author: Edith Stein
text: The individual is only able to find another individual as a living body and as a sensing, feeling, and willing I.

author: Edith Stein
text: Finite being is separated from eternal being, yet every finite being points beyond itself.

author: Gloria Anzaldúa
text: The U.S.-Mexican border es una herida abierta where the Third World grates against the first and bleeds.

author: Gloria Anzaldúa
text: A borderland is a vague and undetermined place created by the emotional residue of an unnatural boundary.

author: Sophie Oluwole
source: Socrates and Ọ̀rúnmìlà: Two Patron Saints of Classical Philosophy (2014)
text: What needs to be characterized and critically examined are African ideas and beliefs… philosophy is about what people say rather than what they do.

author: Sophie Oluwole
text: There is nothing that is absolutely material. There is nothing that is absolutely non-material. And in all phenomenons in the world, the two are there together.

author: Sophie Oluwole
text: It would be ridiculous to raise the question as to whether or not Ọ̀rúnmìlà was religious. He was the leader of a religious cult which established a school structured like Plato's Academy.

author: Sophie Oluwole
source: Punch (Nigeria), interview feature on Sophie Oluwole (2017)
text: Look at Christianity and Islam. They have the Bible and the Koran… Now, where is our own book on Orunmila? It is a question that should worry all rational Yoruba and African people.

author: Audre Lorde
source: "The Master's Tools Will Never Dismantle the Master's House" (1979), in Sister Outsider
text: The master's tools will never dismantle the master's house.

author: Audre Lorde
source: "The Transformation of Silence into Language and Action" (1977), in Sister Outsider
text: Your silence will not protect you.

author: Audre Lorde
source: "Poetry Is Not a Luxury" (1977), in Sister Outsider
text: Poetry is not a luxury. It is a vital necessity of our existence.

author: Al-Farabi
text: The soul has health and sickness just as the body has health and sickness.

author: Al-Farabi
text: The health of the soul is for its traits to be traits by which it does good, fine, and noble actions.

author: Al-Farabi
text: The excellent city is the one in which people cooperate toward the things by which true happiness is attained.

author: Al-Farabi
text: Happiness is the good desired for its own sake; it is never desired for the sake of something else.

author: Al-Farabi
text: The statesman and the king are like the physician: they seek the health of the city as the physician seeks the health of the body.

author: Al-Farabi
source: Enumeration of the Sciences, on political science
text: Political science inquires into the kinds of voluntary actions and ways of life, and into the happiness that is the end of the human being.

author: Avicenna
text: Suppose a person were created at once, fully mature, but with sight veiled and limbs outstretched so that he touched nothing; he would affirm his own existence without affirming any body.

author: Avicenna
text: The Necessary Existent has no cause; rather, It is the cause of all that is possible.

author: Avicenna
text: The knowledge of anything that has causes is not complete unless it is known through its causes.

author: Avicenna
text: The soul is a substance; it is not a body, nor is it impressed in a body as a form in matter in the way of bodily forms.

author: Avicenna
text: The first of intelligibles is the grasp of existence; from it the mind proceeds to the necessary and the possible.

author: Avicenna
text: Prophecy is a perfection of the human intellect joined to a power of imagination that receives and expresses what the intellect knows.

author: Avicenna
text: Medicine is the science by which we learn the various states of the human body in health and when not in health, and the means by which health is likely to be lost and restored.

author: Averroes
text: Wisdom is the companion of the Law and its milk-sister.

author: Averroes
text: The Law has obliged us to reflect upon existing things by means of the intellect, and to seek knowledge of them from that perspective.

author: Averroes
text: If the apparent sense of a scriptural text conflicts with demonstration, that apparent sense admits of allegorical interpretation.

author: Averroes
source: The Decisive Treatise, on the Law’s call to reflection (Butterworth)
text: The Law has urged us to observe beings and directed us to seek knowledge of them by means of demonstration.

author: Averroes
source: The Incoherence of the Incoherence, on causation
text: To deny that things have natures and that from similar natures similar effects follow is to abolish reason and science together.

author: Averroes
text: Assent is of three kinds: rhetorical, dialectical, and demonstrative; people differ in nature as to which kind persuades them.

author: Al-Ghazali
source: The Incoherence of the Philosophers, on causation
text: The connection between what is usually believed to be a cause and what is believed to be an effect is not necessary; each of the two has its own individuality.

author: Al-Ghazali
text: Sense-data are not a secure foundation; the eye sees the star as small, yet demonstration shows it larger than the earth.

author: Al-Ghazali
text: Beyond the intellect there is another stage in which another eye is opened, by which one sees the unseen and what will be in the future.

author: Al-Ghazali
source: The Revival of the Religious Sciences (Iḥyāʾ)
text: Knowledge is not perfected by learning alone; it is perfected when it becomes a state that moves the limbs to action.

author: Al-Ghazali
text: Know yourself, for the knowledge of the self is the key to the knowledge of God.

author: Ibn Tufayl
text: By unaided reason Hayy rose to knowledge of the Necessary Existent, before any human teacher reached him.

author: Ibn Tufayl
text: What revelation teaches by symbols, the philosopher may reach by demonstration; the two agree in substance for those who understand.

author: Ibn Tufayl
text: Most people cling to the outer forms of worship; to strip those forms away suddenly only harms them.

author: Ibn Tufayl
text: Solitude became for him a ladder: withdrawing from the senses, he turned inward toward the Truth.

author: Ibn Khaldun
text: Royal authority and large-scale dynastic power are attained only through group feeling (ʿaṣabiyya).

author: Ibn Khaldun
text: History is a discipline that has a large number of approaches. Its useful aspects are very many. Its goal is distinguished.

author: Ibn Khaldun
text: The past resembles the future more than one drop of water another.

author: Ibn Khaldun
source: Muqaddimah, on the decline of civilization (Rosenthal)
text: When luxury and sedentary culture take hold, group feeling weakens and the dynasty declines.

author: Maimonides
text: Silence and limiting oneself to the apprehensions of the intellect are more appropriate with regard to God than speech.

author: Maimonides
text: The Law as a whole aims at two things: the welfare of the soul and the welfare of the body.

author: Maimonides
text: The more the intellect is perfected, the more one draws near to God; proximity is measured by knowledge.

author: Maimonides
text: The virtues are means between two extremes; the good character is the mean disposition.

author: Maimonides
source: Mishneh Torah, Book of Knowledge (Yesodei ha-Torah)
text: The foundation of all foundations and the pillar of all sciences is to know that there is a First Being who brought every existing thing into being.

author: Maimonides
text: Prophecy is an overflow from God through the intermediation of the Active Intellect, first to the rational faculty and then to the imaginative faculty.

author: Saadia Gaon
source: The Book of Beliefs and Opinions, Introduction (Rosenblatt)
text: God has given us the Torah and also intellect, so that we may verify by reason what we have received by tradition.

author: Saadia Gaon
source: The Book of Beliefs and Opinions (Rosenblatt)
text: Inquiry is not forbidden to us; on the contrary, we are commanded to know God by the path of demonstration as far as we can.

author: Saadia Gaon
source: The Book of Beliefs and Opinions, on creation (Rosenblatt)
text: The world was created ex nihilo; it did not eternally accompany the Creator.

author: Saadia Gaon
source: The Book of Beliefs and Opinions, on reward and punishment (Rosenblatt)
text: Divine justice requires that obedience and disobedience not be equal in outcome; reward and punishment follow desert.

author: Judah Halevi
text: I believe in the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who led the Israelites out of Egypt with signs and miracles—not in the God of Aristotle.

author: Judah Halevi
text: Speculative philosophy may lead to a First Cause, yet it cannot yield the living God who speaks in history and commandment.

author: Judah Halevi
text: Israel among the nations is like the heart among the organs: it is the most sensitive and the most receptive of the divine influence.

author: Kwasi Wiredu
source: "Toward Decolonizing African Philosophy and Religion" (African Studies Quarterly)
text: By decolonization, I mean divesting African philosophical thinking of all undue influences emanating from our colonial past. The crucial word in this formulation is "undue".

author: Kwasi Wiredu
text: A language, most assuredly, is not conceptually neutral; syntax and vocabulary are apt to suggest definite modes of conceptualization.

author: Kwasi Wiredu
source: "The Need for Conceptual Decolonization in African Philosophy" (1995)
text: On the negative side, avoiding or reversing through a critical conceptual self-awareness the unexamined assimilation in our thought of the conceptual frameworks embedded in the foreign philosophical traditions that have had an impact on African life and thought. And, on the positive side, exploiting as much as is judicious the resources of our own indigenous conceptual schemes in our philosophical meditations.

author: Kwasi Wiredu
source: "Democracy and Consensus in African Traditional Politics" (in Cultural Universals and Particulars, 1996)
text: It was a democracy because government was by the consent, and subject to the control, of the people as expressed through their representatives. It was consensual because, at least as a rule, that consent was negotiated on the principle of consensus.

author: Kwasi Wiredu
source: "Democracy and Consensus in African Traditional Politics"
text: By contrast, the majoritarian system might be said to be, in principle, based on consent without consensus.

author: Kwasi Wiredu
source: "The Concept of Truth in the Akan Language" (1985)
text: A theory of truth is not of any real universal significance unless it offers some account of the notion of being so.

author: Kwasi Wiredu
source: Cultural Universals and Particulars (1996), on consensus
text: Governments are not formed by parties but by the consensus of elected representatives. Government becomes a kind of coalition of citizens.

author: Paulin Hountondji
source: African Philosophy: Myth and Reality (Eng. 1983; Fr. 1976)
text: By 'African philosophy' I mean a set of texts, specifically, the set of texts written by Africans and described as philosophical by their authors themselves.

author: Paulin Hountondji
text: So for us African philosophy is a body of literature whose existence is undeniable, a bibliography which has grown constantly.

author: Paulin Hountondji
source: African Philosophy: Myth and Reality (on Tempels)
text: In fact, it is an ethnological work with philosophical pretensions, or more simply, if I may coin the word, a work of 'ethnophilosophy'.

author: Paulin Hountondji
text: I observe that it does exist, by the same right and in the same mode as all the philosophies of the world: in the form of a literature.

author: Paulin Hountondji
text: Contemporary African philosophy, inasmuch as it remains an ethnophilosophy, has been built up essentially for a European public. The African ethnophilosopher's discourse is not intended for Africans.

author: Paulin Hountondji
text: The thought of an African sage, even if he purports to be the spokesman for a group, is not necessarily that of all the individuals in that group, and still less that of all Africans in general.

author: Frantz Fanon
text: O my body, make of me always a man who questions!

author: Frantz Fanon
text: I am not a prisoner of history. I should not seek there for the meaning of my destiny.

author: Frantz Fanon
text: The black man is not. Any more than the white man.

author: Frantz Fanon
text: I am not a slave of Slavery that dehumanized my fathers.

author: Frantz Fanon
source: Black Skin, White Masks, conclusion (Markmann / related Eng.)
text: Superiority? Inferiority? Why not the quite simple attempt to touch the other, to feel the other, to explain the other to myself?

author: Frantz Fanon
text: Each generation must, out of relative obscurity, discover its mission, fulfill it, or betray it.

author: Frantz Fanon
source: "On National Culture", in The Wretched of the Earth
text: National consciousness, which is not nationalism, is the only thing that will give us an international dimension.

author: Léopold Sédar Senghor
source: "Ce que l'homme noir apporte" (1939); Liberté I
text: Emotion is Negro, as reason is Hellenic.

author: Léopold Sédar Senghor
source: standard definition in Senghor's essays on Négritude
text: Négritude is the sum of the cultural values of the black world.

author: Léopold Sédar Senghor
text: The whole system is founded on the notion of vital force. Pre-existing, anterior to being, it constitutes being.

author: Léopold Sédar Senghor
text: The African does not stand outside reality but enters into communion with it; knowledge is participation, not only analysis.

author: Léopold Sédar Senghor
source: essays on the "civilization of the universal"
text: Our ambition is to help build a Civilization of the Universal, a rendezvous of giving and receiving among the cultures of the world.

author: Kwame Anthony Appiah
source: Cosmopolitanism: Ethics in a World of Strangers (2006)
text: Conversation doesn't have to lead to consensus about anything, especially not values; it's enough that it helps people get used to one another.

author: Kwame Anthony Appiah
text: The version of cosmopolitanism that I favor is exactly about balancing universality and difference.

author: Kwame Anthony Appiah
text: Relativism of that sort isn't a way to encourage conversation; it's just a reason to fall silent.

author: Kwame Anthony Appiah
text: A value is like a fax machine: it's not much use if you're the only one who has one.

author: Kwame Anthony Appiah
text: Cosmopolitans begin with a sense of one thing we all certainly share, which is our fallibility. Nobody has reason to be confident that they're right about everything.

author: Kwame Anthony Appiah
text: We have obligations to others that stretch beyond those to whom we are related by ties of kith and kind; and we must take seriously the value not just of human life but of particular human lives.

author: Aimé Césaire
text: A civilization that proves incapable of solving the problems it creates is a decadent civilization.

author: Aimé Césaire
text: A civilization that chooses to close its eyes to its most crucial problems is a stricken civilization. A civilization that uses its principles for trickery and deceit is a dying civilization.

author: Aimé Césaire
text: My turn to state an equation: colonization = "thingification."

author: Aimé Césaire
text: Between colonizer and colonized there is room only for forced labor, intimidation, pressure, the police, taxation, theft, rape… No human contact, but relations of domination and submission.

author: Anton Wilhelm Amo
text: The human mind, insofar as it is a simple substance distinct from the body, can neither suffer from the body nor be confused with it, but by itself, according to its own operations, understands and wills.

author: Anton Wilhelm Amo
source: De humanae mentis apatheia (1734), core thesis
text: Sensation does not belong to the mind; living and sensing belong to the organic body.

author: Anton Wilhelm Amo
source: Tractatus de arte sobrie et accurate philosophandi (1738), related
text: To philosophize soberly and accurately is to distinguish carefully what belongs to the mind from what belongs to the living body.

author: Mogobe B. Ramose
text: Ubuntu is the root of African philosophy. The be-ing of an African in the universe is inseparably anchored upon ubuntu. … Ubuntu then is the wellspring flowing with African ontology and epistemology.

author: Mogobe B. Ramose
text: In spite of decolonisation, the philosophical character of European standpoint on colonisation together with its corresponding practices remains unchanged in its relations with the erstwhile colonies. It is precisely this condition which calls for the need for the authentic liberation of Africa.

author: Mogobe B. Ramose
source: "An African perspective on justice and race" (polylog); Ubuntu ethics
text: Ubuntu is the principle that we act humanely and with respect towards others as a way of demanding the same from them.

author: Mogobe B. Ramose
source: African Philosophy Through Ubuntu (on umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu)
text: To be a human being is to affirm one's humanity by recognising the humanity of others and, on that basis, establish humane relations with them.

author: Kwasi Wiredu
text: The African who has learned philosophy in English, for example, has most likely become conceptually westernized to a large extent not by choice but by the force of historical circumstances.

author: Frantz Fanon
source: "On National Culture", in The Wretched of the Earth
text: It is at the heart of national consciousness that international consciousness lives and grows.

author: Paulin Hountondji
text: Philosophy, by definition, is an individual critical activity; the myth of a collective, unanimous African philosophy must be discarded.

author: Kwame Anthony Appiah
source: Cosmopolitanism: Ethics in a World of Strangers；cf. “The Case for Contamination, ” NYT Magazine (1 Jan 2006)
text: They know they don't have all the answers. They're humble enough to think that they might learn from strangers; not too humble to think that strangers can't learn from them.

author: Aimé Césaire
source: Discours sur la Négritude (Miami, Feb 1987); Eng. in SEP “Négritude”
text: Négritude, in my eyes, is not a philosophy. Négritude is not a metaphysics. … It is a way of living history within history.

author: Kwasi Wiredu
source: "The Concept of Truth in the Akan Language"
text: There is no one word in Akan for truth.

author: Nishida Kitaro
source: "The Logic of the Place of Nothingness and the Religious Worldview, " in Last Writings (Dilworth, p. 91)
text: There must be an overturning, a radical conversion of mind, in any religion. Without it there is no religion.

author: Nishida Kitaro
text: The religious consciousness does not arise out of our own selves; it is simultaneously the call of God or Buddha.

author: Nishida Kitaro
text: Compassion always signifies that opposites are one in the dynamic reciprocity of their own contradictory identity. The religious will arise as the self-determination of this dimension of sympathetic coalescence.

author: Nishitani Keiji
source: Religion and Nothingness, trans. Jan Van Bragt, p. 3
text: For what purpose do I exist?

author: Nishitani Keiji
text: At the point of our deepest questioning of ourselves, the religious quest awakens in us.

author: Nishitani Keiji
text: So long as the field of separation between within and without is not broken through, and so long as a conversion from that standpoint does not take place, the lack of unity and contradiction spoken of earlier cannot help but prevail among the things we take as real.

author: Nishitani Keiji
source: Religion and Nothingness (Van Bragt; discussion of śūnyatā)
text: Nothingness in the sense of emptiness (śūnyatā) is not separate from being, but always in a relationship with being: being-sive-nothingness, nothingness-sive-being.

author: Nishitani Keiji
source: Religion and Nothingness (Van Bragt, opening discussion of religion)
text: Religion cannot be fully understood either within the parameters of utility or from a sociological viewpoint alone.

author: Watsuji Tetsuro
source: Rinrigaku: Ethics in Japan, trans. Yamamoto & Carter, p. 10
text: The locus of ethical problems lies not in the consciousness of the isolated individual, but precisely in the in-betweenness of person and person.

author: Watsuji Tetsuro
text: Ethics is, in the final analysis, the study of ningen — the human person as both individual and social, as “betweenness.”

author: Watsuji Tetsuro
source: Climate and Culture (Fūdo), trans. Geoffrey Bownas, p. 1
text: Fūdo means wind and earth — the natural environment of a given land.

author: Watsuji Tetsuro
source: Climate and Culture (Bownas; intentional experience of cold)
text: We discover ourselves in the cold — and in the same moment we discover the cold in ourselves — before any sharp division of subject and object.

author: Nagarjuna
text: Whatever is dependently co-arisen, that is explained to be emptiness. That, being a dependent designation, is itself the middle way.

author: Nagarjuna
text: Neither from itself nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause, does anything whatever, anywhere arise.

author: Nagarjuna
text: There is not the slightest difference between cyclic existence and nirvana. There is not the slightest difference between nirvana and cyclic existence.

author: Nagarjuna
text: Something that is not dependently arisen — such a thing does not exist. Therefore a non-empty thing does not exist.

author: Dignaga
text: Perception is free from conceptual construction.

author: Dignaga
source: Pramāṇasamuccaya (two instruments of knowledge; standard summary)
text: There are only two instruments of knowledge: perception and inference.

author: Leopoldo Zea
source: cited in SEP “Latin American Philosophy: Metaphilosophical Foundations” (Zea 1948, p. 226)
text: The abstract issues [of philosophy] will have to be seen from the Latin American man’s own circumstance. … When we [Latin Americans] address abstract issues, we shall formulate them as issues of our own.

author: Leopoldo Zea
text: If we are to be faithful to our calling, we have to affirm that our situation is not that of Jean-Paul Sartre. Our situation is not that of the European bourgeoisie.

author: Leopoldo Zea
source: Filosofía de la historia americana (FHA), p. 88 (Eng. rendering via Reichl 2025)
text: Because man had been slave he cannot enslave without negating himself.

author: Enrique Dussel
text: Before the ego cogito there is an ego conquiro; “I conquer” is the practical foundation of “I think.”

author: Enrique Dussel
text: From the “I conquer” applied to the Aztec and Inca world and all America, from the “I enslave” applied to Africans … from this “I” appears the Cartesian ego cogito.

author: Enrique Dussel
text: Philosophy, when it is really philosophy and not sophistry or ideology, does not ponder philosophy. … Philosophy ponders the nonphilosophical; the reality.

author: Enrique Dussel
text: Written from the periphery, for persons and peoples of the periphery, this book nonetheless also addresses readers in the center of the present world system.

author: David Hume
text: Be a philosopher; but amidst all your philosophy, be still a man.

author: Aristotle
text: Virtue, then, is a state of character concerned with choice, lying in a mean, i.e. the mean relative to us, this being determined by a rational principle, and by that principle by which the man of practical wisdom would determine it.

author: Zhang Zai
text: Heaven is my father and Earth is my mother, and even such a small creature as I finds an intimate place in their midst.

author: Zhang Zai
text: The Great Void has no physical form; it is the original substance of qi. Its gathering and dispersing are but the passing forms of change.

author: Huineng
text: It is not the wind that moves; it is not the flag that moves; it is your mind that moves.

author: Huineng
text: The Buddhist teaching is in the world; awakening is not apart from the world. To seek enlightenment apart from the world is like looking for a hare's horn.

author: Linji Yixuan
text: If you meet the Buddha, kill the Buddha; if you meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch; if you meet an arhat, kill the arhat.

author: Linji Yixuan
text: There is a true person of no rank who is always coming and going through the gates of your face.

author: Linji Yixuan
text: There is no place in Buddhism for special effort. Just be ordinary: put on your clothes, eat your food, and lie down when you are tired.

author: George Berkeley
source: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge, §1
text: It is evident to any one who takes a survey of the objects of human knowledge, that they are either ideas actually imprinted on the senses; or else such as are perceived by attending to the passions and operations of the mind; or lastly, ideas formed by help of memory and imagination.

author: George Berkeley
source: Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous (1713)
text: That neither our thoughts, nor passions, nor ideas formed by the imagination, exist without the mind, is what everybody will allow.

author: George Berkeley
source: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge, §27
text: A spirit is one simple, undivided, active being: as it perceives ideas, it is called understanding, and as it produces or otherwise operates about ideas, it is called will.

author: Gabriel Marcel
text: To love a being is to say: thou, thou shalt not die.

author: Gabriel Marcel
text: A mystery is a problem which encroaches upon its own data, invading them, as it were, and thereby transcending itself as a mere problem.

author: Wang Guowei
source: Renjian Cihua (Remarks on Lyrics in the Human World), §1
text: Ci poetry takes jingjie — the aesthetic realm — as its highest: with jingjie it naturally attains a lofty style and famous lines of its own.

author: Wang Guowei
text: Jingjie is not a matter of scenery alone: joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness are also realms of the human heart. Whoever can write true scenery and true feeling may be said to have jingjie.

author: Mozi
text: To kill one man is called unrighteousness and incurs one capital crime; by this reckoning, to kill ten men is ten times unrighteous and incurs ten capital crimes.

author: Mozi
text: The task of the humane is to promote the benefit of all under Heaven and to eliminate its harm.

author: Feng Youlan
source: A Short History of Chinese Philosophy
